title: Parental Responses to Youth Disclosure: How Guilt Induction Shapes Future Communication and Actions
abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction Youth disclosure is the primary way parents gain knowledge about their adolescent children; it is linked with better youth adjustment and encouraged by supportive parenting. When youth disclose a transgression, parents may feel torn between stressing wrongdoing to reduce misbehavior and responding neutrally to maintain future disclosure. This study employed vignettes to investigate how social domain and parental responses influence adolescents' expected future disclosure and behavior while exploring evaluations of parental responses as explanatory variables. Methods U.S. undergraduate students ( N = 358, M age = 19.76, SD = 1.48; 77% female) evaluated vignettes about disclosing a behavior to a parent as a teen. Behaviors varied by domain (moral, prudential, multifaceted, personal); parental guilt‐inductive statements varied by criticism focus (person or behavior) and highlighted harm (parent or direct). Participants rated how parental responses would have affected their future disclosure, (mis)behavior, feelings of rejection, guilt, and shame, and evaluated responses' acceptability. Results Neutral responses reduced expected future disclosure the least, followed by behavior‐critical responses (especially those highlighting direct harm), which suppressed future disclosure less than person‐critical responses for all but personal issues. Behavior‐critical responses were most effective at reducing expected future (mis)behavior, with the strongest reductions across responses for moral and prudential issues. Effects on acceptability, felt rejection, and felt guilt/shame help explain the primary findings. Conclusions Parents may balance reducing problem behavior while maintaining open communication by responding to adolescents' disclosure with inductive statements focusing on the direct, negative effects of the misbehavior rather than criticizing the adolescent as a person.
